specPoints.text: know that the mole(mol) is the unit for the amount of a substance
understand how to carry out calculations involving amount of substance, relative atomic mass $ (A_{r}) $ and relative formula mass $ (M_{r}) $

primer.text: You already met relative atomic mass (Ar) in Atomic Structure, where it compares the mass of an atom with the carbon-12 scale. You can also write formulae such as H2O and NaCl and add atomic masses to find a compound's relative formula mass. This note adds the mole, the bridge between the masses you can weigh and the numbers of particles that react.

lessons.title: The Mole
lessons.opening: Bundles make counting practical. Paper is sold in reams and eggs in dozens, and chemists bundle particles in the same spirit: one mole is a fixed count of particles, 6.02 × 10^23 of them. Because every mole holds the same count, one mole of different substances generally has a different mass — a value called the molar mass.
keyPoints: Chemical amounts are counted in moles, and the mole (mol) is the accepted unit of amount of substance.
Equal amounts in moles contain equal numbers of particles, whatever the substance.
The number of particles in one mole is the Avogadro constant, 6.02 × 10^23 per mole.
The mass of one mole is the molar mass: for an element it matches the relative atomic mass in grams.
For a compound, the molar mass matches the relative formula mass in grams, found by adding the atomic masses together.

low.restatement: A mole is simply a fixed number of particles: 6.02 × 10^23 of them, the same count for every substance. The mass of that count is the molar mass, and for an element it equals the relative atomic mass written in grams.
low.analogy: Think of a dozen. A dozen eggs and a dozen oranges hold the same count but weigh differently; a mole of carbon and a mole of helium also hold the same count but weigh 12 g and 4 g.
low.examPointer: Questions may ask how many particles sit in a mole of atoms, molecules, ions or electrons — the count is identical, so always name the particle type in the answer.

medium.restatement: The mole (mol) is the unit of amount of substance: one mole of any species contains 6.02 × 10^23 of the particles stated, whether atoms, molecules, ions or formula units. Molar mass links that count to grams, matching Ar for elements and Mr for compounds.
medium.analogy: A bank counting notes in bundles still cares which currency it holds; a chemist counting particles in moles still cares whether the bundle contains sodium atoms or hydrogen molecules.
medium.examPointer: Expect a comparison item such as: one mole of carbon holds as many atoms as there are molecules in one mole of carbon dioxide — state the particle type, then apply the Avogadro constant.

check.stem: Which quantity does one mole measure?

options.explanation: The mole counts how much substance is present, and every mole holds the same number of particles.
Mass is measured in grams and differs between substances, while a mole fixes only the particle count.
options.misconception: treats the mole as a unit of mass

options.explanation: Volume is a separate quantity; the mole counts particles without fixing a volume at this stage of the course.
options.misconception: confuses the mole with molar volume

options.explanation: Reactivity is a chemical property unrelated to how much is present.
options.misconception: links amount of substance to reactivity

check.stem: How many atoms are present in one mole of helium?
check.misconceptionClass: Avogadro constant value and particle-type slips

options.explanation: One mole of any particles contains the Avogadro constant of them, so one mole of helium atoms is 6.02 × 10^23 atoms.
The exponent is positive: the constant is 6.02 × 10^23 per mole, a vast count rather than a tiny fraction.
options.misconception: inverts the exponent of the Avogadro constant

options.explanation: A mole is a bundle of 6.02 × 10^23 particles, not a single one.
options.misconception: treats the mole as a single particle

options.explanation: The answer must name particles; moles of moles is a unit error.
options.misconception: recurses the unit instead of naming the particles counted

check.stem: One mole of carbon and one mole of helium are compared. Which statement is true?

options.text: They contain the same number of atoms
options.explanation: Equal moles contain equal particle counts; only the masses differ, 12 g against 4 g.
The masses follow the relative atomic masses, 12 g for carbon and 4 g for helium.
options.misconception: assumes equal moles must have equal masses

options.text: Carbon contains twice as many atoms
options.explanation: Particle count depends only on the number of moles, not on how heavy each atom is.
options.misconception: scales particle count with atomic mass

options.text: Helium contains more atoms because its atoms are lighter
options.explanation: Lighter atoms simply make a lighter mole; the count per mole is fixed for every substance.
options.misconception: believes lighter particles pack more of them into one mole

check.stem: What is the mass of one mole of lithium? (Ar: Li = 7)

options.explanation: The molar mass of an element equals its relative atomic mass written in grams.
Molar mass is read in grams, not kilograms.
options.misconception: swaps grams for kilograms when converting Ar to molar mass

options.explanation: The Avogadro constant counts particles; it is not a mass.
options.misconception: substitutes the Avogadro constant for the molar mass

options.text: It cannot be found without more data
options.explanation: Ar alone fixes the molar mass of an element; no extra data is needed.
options.misconception: believes molar mass requires experimental data beyond Ar

check.stem: Which value is the molar mass of water, H2O? (Ar: H = 1, O = 16)

options.explanation: Molar mass = (2 × 1) + 16 = 18 g per mole.
Only the hydrogen is doubled: (2 × 1) + 16 = 18, not 2 × (1 + 16) = 34.
options.misconception: multiplies every atomic mass by the subscript instead of only the atom it follows

options.explanation: The formula H2O carries two hydrogen atoms, so both must be added.
options.misconception: counts only one hydrogen atom in the formula

options.explanation: The oxygen contribution alone is 16 g; hydrogen adds 2 g more.
options.misconception: ignores the hydrogen contribution entirely

lessons.title: Moles-Mass Calculations
lessons.opening: Balances cannot weigh out one mole directly, yet reactions happen particle by particle in fixed molar ratios. The way through is arithmetic: one relationship links moles, mass in grams and molar mass, and it works in both directions. Master the rearrangement once and every moles-mass question becomes two lines of working.
keyPoints: Reactions happen in molar ratios, but laboratory balances read grams, so converting between the two units is unavoidable.
One relationship links the quantities: moles = mass ÷ molar mass.
Rearranged the same way, mass = moles × molar mass.
Molar mass carries the unit g mol^-1 and is numerically equal to Ar for an element or Mr for a compound.
Standard form keeps very small or large answers readable, such as 7.71 × 10^-3 mol for 2.64 g of sucrose.

low.restatement: To find moles, divide the mass by the molar mass; to find mass, multiply the moles by the molar mass. Watch the units as a direction check: g mol^-1 cancels grams to leave moles.
low.analogy: Coins come in rolls of a fixed mass. Weighing a bag of rolls and dividing by the mass of one roll tells you how many rolls you have — the same move as grams divided by g mol^-1.
low.examPointer: Write the relationship before substituting numbers and show every step; method marks survive an arithmetic slip, while a bare answer does not.

medium.restatement: Amount in moles = mass in grams ÷ molar mass in g mol^-1, where molar mass equals Ar for an element and Mr for a compound; rearranging gives mass = moles × molar mass. Quote very small or very large answers in standard form to three significant figures.
medium.analogy: A currency converter uses one exchange rate in two directions, pounds to euros or the reverse; the moles-mass relationship is that single rate, and molar mass is the published figure on the board.
medium.examPointer: Stems often supply Mr directly, as with 2.64 g of sucrose at Mr 342.3; divide, then present the answer in standard form with the unit mol still visible.

check.stem: Why must a chemist convert between grams and moles?

options.text: Balances measure grams while reactions proceed in molar ratios
options.explanation: The balance reads grams, but reacting quantities are fixed particle-for-particle, so a conversion is always needed.
Balances measure solids perfectly well in grams; the issue is the unit, not the sample type.
options.misconception: misstates what laboratory balances can do

options.explanation: Moles count particles of solids, liquids and gases alike.
options.misconception: restricts the mole to one state of matter

options.text: Grams are only used for products
options.explanation: Both reactants and products are weighed in grams; the mole is needed for both sides of an equation.
options.misconception: splits the measurement unit by reaction role

check.stem: Which expression gives the number of moles in a sample of mass m whose molar mass is M?

options.explanation: Moles = mass ÷ molar mass; dividing grams by g mol^-1 leaves moles.
Dividing the molar mass by the mass gives the reciprocal quantity.
options.misconception: inverts the moles-mass relationship

options.explanation: Multiplication is the mass-from-moles direction, not moles-from-mass.
options.misconception: multiplies where division is required

options.explanation: Subtracting unlike quantities has no meaning here; the relationship is multiplicative.
options.misconception: guesses an operation instead of using the relationship

check.stem: What is the mass of 0.250 mol of zinc? (Ar: Zn = 65.38)

options.explanation: Mass = 0.250 × 65.38 = 16.345, which rounds to 16.3 g at three significant figures.
That value comes from dividing moles by molar mass; the mass direction multiplies.
options.misconception: divides moles by molar mass instead of multiplying

options.explanation: Adding the mole amount to the molar mass mixes two different quantities.
options.misconception: adds the molar mass to the mole amount

options.explanation: The product is 16.345; a factor-of-ten slip inflates it.
options.misconception: slips a decimal place when multiplying

check.stem: How many moles are in 2.64 g of sucrose, C12H22O11 (Mr = 342.3)?

options.explanation: Moles = 2.64 ÷ 342.3 = 0.0077125 mol, which is 7.71 × 10^-3 mol at three significant figures.
That value comes from dividing the molar mass by the mass; the mole direction is the reverse.
options.misconception: divides the molar mass by the mass

options.explanation: Multiplying mass by molar mass answers the wrong question entirely.
options.misconception: multiplies mass by molar mass

options.explanation: The quotient is 0.0077125; the decimal point sits one position too high here.
options.misconception: places the decimal point one position too high

check.stem: What mass is 0.100 mol of sodium chloride, NaCl? (Mr: NaCl = 58.5)

options.explanation: Dividing instead of multiplying answers the moles question, not the mass question.
options.misconception: divides mass by molar mass when mass was asked for

options.explanation: 58.5 g is the mass of one whole mole, but the sample holds only 0.100 mol.
options.misconception: reports the molar mass instead of the sample mass

options.explanation: The product is 5.85; a factor-of-ten slip inflates it.
options.misconception: slips a decimal place in the multiplication

glossary.definition: The unit of amount of substance in chemistry; one mole contains 6.02 × 10^23 of the stated particles.
The number of particles in one mole of any substance, equal to 6.02 × 10^23 per mole.
The mass of one mole of a substance in grams per mole; numerically the Ar of an element or the Mr of a compound.
The mass of one atom of an element measured against the carbon-12 scale.
The particle counted for an ionic compound, matching the ratio of ions shown in its formula.
The total of the relative atomic masses added across a compound's formula.
A way of writing very large or very small numbers as a multiplier and a power of ten.

workedExample.prompt: Both worked examples from the note body, one per direction of the moles-mass relationship: (1) What is the mass of 0.250 moles of zinc? (2) How many moles are in 2.64 g of sucrose, C12H22O11 (Mr = 342.3)?
steps: Example 1 — mass from moles: the molar mass of zinc equals its relative atomic mass, 65.38 g mol^-1.
Example 1 — mass is found by multiplying moles by molar mass: 0.250 × 65.38 = 16.3 (3 s.f.).
Example 2 — moles from mass: the molar mass of sucrose is 342.3 g mol^-1.
Example 2 — moles are found by dividing mass by molar mass: 2.64 ÷ 342.3 = 7.71 × 10^-3 mol (3 s.f.).
workedExample.finalAnswer: 16.3 g of zinc (3 s.f.); 7.71 × 10^-3 mol of sucrose (3 s.f.)
